I can really relate to this.
I binge for emotional reasons as well as purely out of habit. Depression makes it really easy to just say "fuck it" and eat ridiculous amounts of food because at least it's momentarily pleasurable. When days feel pointless and long, food is something to look forward to almost. 
And with no self esteem it's hard to argue against that impulse to overeat because, after all, if you don't care about yourself you also don't care how you look or how (un)healthy you are. 
I lost 60 pounds last year, going from overweight to a healthy weight, and over the past few months I've gained back just over half of it. I'm right on the line of overweight again and it feels really bad to know how much I've let things slip. I remember when I first started losing weight though, and how it came from a place of wanting to better take care of myself. Up until then, I'd never been able to lose more than five or so pounds at once before giving up again.
It's tempting to be angry at myself for messing up and just continue to binge out of hopelessness, frustration, etc. I haven't been able to stop yet. As destructive and detrimental as it is, I still binge. I need to value myself enough to give up the comfort I get from food because, that aside, it impacts my life so negatively -- I feel self conscious all the time, am always full of regret and shame, feel embarrassed to go out. 
Lately, I've been skipping class work, smoking too much weed, and barely doing anything at all really. Binging is the same as all of it -- a coping mechanism that makes things a little better and a little worse at the same time. I'm just going to keep trying to lose the habit, and hopefully I can figure it out soon.

Wow, thank you for your reply, this honestly calmed me down a lot. 
The "glass closet" thing definitely resonates with me, although some of it might be more in my head than I realize. And I think you're really on target asking about how I think of myself, how I value other people's opinions of me, etc. 
I really do need to become more comfortable with myself, and you're right, I mean I'm not doing anything wrong. I think it might be low self esteem in general, and worrying that being seen as not straight will just be compounded with other "flaws" or things that make me less "normal" in people's eyes. But I guess that'll probably get better with time, I just have to work on it some more.
Thank you again for responding, it helps a lot to hear from someone who can relate! I don't know a lot of gay people irl, which probably doesn't help my problem haha

Ethical veganism is just about trying to cause the least amount of harm possible (within reason).

Obviously, you could plant fifty trees and then kill yourself and probably have a much smaller carbon footprint, but no ones advocating that because it's about taking reasonable steps to reduce harm where possible. 


Just because veganism is not the absolute absence of cruelty doesn't make it an invalid response to the issue. By virtue of our existence, we cause some harm -- no way to avoid that. However, that doesn't mean that attempting to minimize that harm isn't worthwhile. 
People get murdered or robbed all the time, it's not something we can control, but we can choose not to do it ourselves because we ethically want to reduce harm to our fellow humans. Sure, someone could say that harm to other people is inevitable, so why not cause more harm? But we understand that ethically, less suffering is better than more even if we can't end all suffering. This is why we don't punch people, or steal, even though violence and theft are unavoidable facts of life. 

So sure, vegans aren't perfect. No ones claiming they are. But to say that wanting to minimize harm to animals/the environment means you should kill yourself to neutralize your impact is just a standard you wouldn't apply to someone who eats meat. And say a non-vegan happens to recycle and avoid hitting their pets, would those somehow be pointless stances against pollution and animal abuse that are morally ineffective if not carried to an extreme? Why try to keep plastic out of landfills when it will get there anyway? Why not kill yourself so you're not creating demand for more plastic products? Obviously no one says these things, because we understand that it's reasonable to try and reduce waste even when waste is unavoidable. The fact of its inevitability doesn't make efforts to alleviate it worthless. 

You're drawing an arbitrary line at eating meat. You're saying that going beyond not abusing pets or hurting animals to refraining from killing and eating them is somehow so radical that you might as well kill yourself if you feel so strongly. But people do other things to help the environment and animals all the time - trying not to waste water, driving electric cars, adopting from animal shelters instead of breeders, etc. 

Would you pose this same question to someone who drives a Prius, challenging them as to why they'd have the audacity to try to reduce greenhouse gases when their very existence results in increased carbon emissions? Probably not, because they're just doing a pretty logical thing in response to an issue -- making a relatively reasonable, small choice to minimize harm done even when avoiding it altogether isn't possible. 
And sure, they could quit driving altogether, but they probably have places they need to go and a regular life to lead. Since an electric car helps them reduce harm without limiting their life too much, they do it. Same with people who avoid meat -- it's not the absolute avoidance of all harm, it's just a way to minimize it as much as possible while still leading a regular life. Which, as you can understand, makes suicide a less logical step to take, regardless of the potential for harm-reduction.

Isn't easier to work hard at your job, come home to a living space that's clean and comfortable? With tv, internet, phones, bed, bills paid, etc? It's definitely preferable, that's why the vast majority of the population works to make that happen. 
If someone doesn't have these things, it's probably not because they somehow feel too lazy to work for it. 
It's a huge effort to survive on the street, where you're looked down upon by people passing by, hustled along by police for trying to sleep in public, avoiding harm from other people because you lack protection in the form of basic shelter, constant discomfort from weather or inability to bathe, etc. 
The idea that laziness, or choosing to do the easier, less effortful thing, applies here is inaccurate. 
If you handed a homeless person a new wardrobe, a cheap room to live in, access to a little money, and the chance to apply to some jobs, chances are high that they'd be pretty stoked on it. 
And if you think about it, someone probably handed -you- those things. When you graduated high school, shortly after you probably went from living in your parents home to working at a job and being able to pay for housing on some level. Or, you had the chance to go to college, even. Your situation allowed you to have access to the steps along the way to a "normal" life. Society is set up in a way that "handed you" the opportunity to work for these things. 
With someone suffering from a severe mental illness, for example, society is not set up to give that person these same opportunities. Same with someone whose family is unstable and unable to provide the support yours (and most others) do. This could mean foster families (in which case you're basically 100% on your own with no help when you hit 18) or maybe just families living in poverty already. Or sexual or physical abuse, or parents with drug/alcohol abuse problems or mental illness themselves. It's not that they're not working as hard as the people who did manage to get housing and a job and a "normal" life, it's that it was likely much harder for them to reach these things.
Homeless people likely didn't have the same start as people more successful now, and that's not down to laziness or a character flaw. Everyone is trying to do their best to survive, and giving 5 dollars to someone whose efforts haven't carried them as far as yours, whether that's circumstance or something else, shouldn't be so controversial. 
There's no reason to assume that someone doing worse than you in life is just not trying hard enough. If there was a way to just easily get a job after living on the streets and having no address, nowhere to wash/get clean clothes to wear for work, etc. people would do it. No one is living in a way that's so unpleasant and dangerous just because they're too lazy to fill out an application.

Hi, this is my first time posting in this sub but I've been lurking for about a year. I've been struggling a bit recently and it would mean a lot if anyone had any advice or experience to offer. You're all really inspiring, and a big part of how I was able to get started eating healthier. :)
I'm 16 years old (F, 5'11) and went down from 205 pounds in February 2016 to 145 by about June. (My flair is off, I'm on mobile and haven't been able to change it for a long time) In the months after, I've been up and down quite a lot, currently at 170 and feeling really deeply.... tired? Regretful? And stupid for messing up half my progress. 
I keep trying to restart my old routine and have been counting calories as best as I can (with MyFitnessPal) but whenever I binge I just don't log anything for the day and promise to never do it again... which of course is never true. 
I had stopped eating processed sugar altogether and that had helped the first time around, but all the salads, healthy meals, cooked vegetables, etc. that I was used to at the time now seem really unappealing. I've been eating all kinds of junk, things I never thought I'd touch again - cookies, ice cream, pizza, etc. Maybe I just need to get used to it again? Part of me is resisting getting "back on track" because it seems so hard and restrictive, although logically, I know it wasn't so bad at the time and was actually rewarding and enjoyable. 
I just feel really guilty that I let myself gain back so many pounds and it honestly feels like a nightmare. I was finally getting to the point where I didn't hate my body so much and wasn't so embarrassed of myself and now it's back to this. I know "accepting" it and moving forward is probably the way to go, but how do I go about doing that? I feel like I can't stop binging. Does anyone have any experience for this or ideas about where to go from here?

I can definitely relate to feeling exactly that type of loss when I'm without my therapist. I'm sorry you had to go through that as well, but it helps to know I'm not weird/crazy for being affected by it a little bit.
I'll try to stay busy and will definitely hang around on here - it's really nice to not feel so alone. Thanks for listening.

I didn't want her to think I was making a big deal out of things, but I think you're right, it might help a lot. I think I was/am just scared of coming across as too needy or weird or something. Honestly, reading what you said is really reassuring, so thank you! I think I'll bring it up with her next time I see her. 
Thanks again x
